snippets.text: Staphylococcus epidermidis is a common symbiont bacterium that can become infectious once inside the human host. They are among the most common causes of nosocomial infection in the United States and can lead to serious complications. This activity reviews the evaluation and treatment of Staphylococcus epidermidis infection and explains the role of the interprofessional team in managing patients with this condition.

snippets.text: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is a severe dermatologic condition caused by a systemic infection with toxin-producing staphylococcal bacteria. This condition primarily affects children and immunocompromised adults, leading to widespread skin desquamation and erythema that mimics other severe dermatologic conditions, such as Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. The extent of skin involvement varies, with some individuals exhibiting localized forms due to preexisting antibodies while others experience full-body exfoliation. Loss of the protective skin barrier places patients at risk for complications, including hypothermia, dehydration from fluid loss, and secondary infections. Diagnosis is largely clinical but may be supported by laboratory and histologic studies. Treatment typically includes inpatient care with intravenous antibiotics, fluid replacement, and close monitoring for potential complications and relapse.

snippets.text: The diagnosis of an acute infection is eminently clinical: inflammation, flushing, increased temperature, fluctuation, purulent drainage or dehiscence of the surgical wound, accompanied or not by systemic symptoms such as general malaise and fever, with analytical data (leucocytosis, elevated C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate) supporting the diagnosis. In terms of culture collection, it is preferable to take deep cultures (five samples) during surgical debridement; if performed superficially, there is a risk of skin germ contamination.

Onset is sudden, with fever (39° to 40.5°C, which remains elevated), hypotension, a diffuse macular

erythroderma, and involvement of at least 2 other organ systems.

Staphylococcal TSS is likely to cause vomiting, diarrhea, myalgia, elevated CK, mucositis, hepatic

damage, thrombocytopenia, and confusion. The staphylococcal TSS rash is more likely to desquamate,

particularly on the palms and soles, between 3 and 7 days after onset.

Streptococcal TSS commonly causes respiratory distress syndrome, coagulopathy, and hepatic damage

and is more likely to cause fever, malaise, and severe pain at the site of a soft-tissue infection.

Renal impairment is frequent and common to both. The syndrome may progress within 48 h to syncope,

shock, and death. Less severe cases of staphylococcal TSS are fairly common.
